body:
why I was fired
[](https://act.lucaskunce.com/go/105464?refcode=em20260619-10585&firstname=Peter&lastname=Willis&email=dpwillis67@gmail.com&zip=18326&city=Cresco&state=PA&amounts=5%2C20%2C50%2C100%2C250%2C500%2C1000&t=1&akid=10585%2E614464%2Ewy6QsO)
In October 2021, I had been an employee of Kellogg’s for almost 18 years.
I had dropped out of college and gone to work for the company after my wife got pregnant. Life’s easy when all you gotta do is take care of yourself – but we needed diapers and health insurance for our growing family.
Working at Kellogg’s used to be a lifelong career. A good-paying job that let you become a homeowner, live decently, and hopefully retire some day.
But over the years, that changed. Workers were paid less. Cost of living adjustments weren’t keeping up anywhere near inflation. Retirement and health insurance plans were gutted. It just wasn’t right. They were making record profits – and doing it off the backs of workers.
**So in October 2021, we walked out. And as president of our local union, I led the strike.**
[](https://act.lucaskunce.com/go/105464?refcode=em20260619-10585&firstname=Peter&lastname=Willis&email=dpwillis67@gmail.com&zip=18326&city=Cresco&state=PA&amounts=5%2C20%2C50%2C100%2C250%2C500%2C1000&t=2&akid=10585%2E614464%2Ewy6QsO)
Most of us had never walked a picket line. It was cold, but we were determined to hold our lines through the dead of the winter if we had to. We were a part of something bigger than ourselves. We were in a fight for the future of the American middle class.
After 11 weeks in the cold, we reached an agreement. More importantly, we saved 500 good-paying union jobs.
It was one of the proudest moments of my life.
[](https://act.lucaskunce.com/go/105464?refcode=em20260619-10585&firstname=Peter&lastname=Willis&email=dpwillis67@gmail.com&zip=18326&city=Cresco&state=PA&amounts=5%2C20%2C50%2C100%2C250%2C500%2C1000&t=3&akid=10585%2E614464%2Ewy6QsO)
Following the strike, I was fired. Someone had to pay – and as union president, my head was on the chopping block.
It’s easy to let yourself get beaten down by life. To let big corporations and the politicians they own in Washington make all the decisions – and just accept that that’s how things will always be. But that’s not me.
Instead, I decided last year to run against one of the most corporate politicians – U.S. Senator Republican Deb Fischer – and we nearly won. I got 47% of the vote in one of the closest Senate races in the country.
**Now, I’m running again for the U.S. Senate – this time against billionaire Republican Pete Ricketts – and the first poll shows us virtually TIED: 46% to 45%.**
I am taking on a literal billionaire senator. We can finish what we started last year and flip Nebraska’s Senate seat for working class people, but I need grassroots donors like you to give now if we’re going to win this seat.

subject: I lost a pregnancy. The pain management was medieval.
disclaimer_text: PAID FOR BY MGP VICTORY FUND, A JOINT
body:
https://secure.actblue.com/donate/mgpvf-dsg-email? [https://secure.actblue.com/donate/mgpvf-dsg-email?]
A few weeks ago, my husband and I lost a pregnancy.
The physical toll was something not even my doctor prepared me for.
After 11 weeks of hope about bringing a new member into our family, we learned the pregnancy was no longer viable. After several weeks of bleeding and mourning, my doctor made clear that future pregnancy could be much more difficult if I didn't take medication to expel the retained miscarriage.
Like most women, I was told the medication would feel like a regular period. Maybe a little stronger cramping.
But when I took the medication, the pain was more intense than the pain I experienced delivering my son four years ago. I wasn't even advised to take it when my son was out of the house.
And I am not alone.

name: Elissa Slotkin
subject: On Juneteenth

body:
# [](https://act.elissaslotkin.org/go/188?t=1&akid=2472%2E135344%2E2YpaYc)

One of the easiest and most rewarding votes I’ve taken as a member of Congress was in June 2021, when Juneteenth officially became a federal holiday. It marks the end of slavery in the United States and honors the struggle and sacrifice that it took to secure that freedom.
As a big history nerd, I can’t let the day pass without a very brief rendition of the story of Juneteenth and what it means to Michigan today.
Today marks the 161st anniversary of June 19th, 1865, when Union troops arrived in Galveston Bay, Texas, with news of freedom, nearly 2 years after the Emancipation Proclamation. The day would be known as Freedom Day, as former slaves rejoiced.
And while Juneteenth began in Texas, the tradition has spread across the country, including here in Michigan too. Early celebrations of emancipation in Michigan were held on August 1, the anniversary of a speech Frederick Douglass gave in Battle Creek on the perils of ignoring history. For many years, August 1st was celebrated annually. It wasn’t until the Civil Rights Movement that Juneteenth became more widespread. Though the holiday had been celebrated for decades by that point, Detroit officially started celebrating Juneteenth in the 1990s.
This year, I will be celebrating by visiting The Charles H. Wright Museum of African American History in Detroit, an extraordinary space and the nation's largest institution dedicated exclusively to African American history and culture.
Amidst the celebrations, I hope you’ll join me in taking some time today for reflection and honoring those who fought for Black freedom in America by continuing their fight. It is an important milestone, and a reminder that the fight for justice and equality is never over.
Thank you,
Elissa

The day would be known as Freedom Day, as former slaves rejoiced. And while Juneteenth began in Texas, the tradition has spread across the country, including here in Michigan too. Early celebrations of emancipation in Michigan were held on August 1, the anniversary of a speech Frederick Douglass gave in Battle Creek on the perils of ignoring history. For many years, August 1st was celebrated annually. It wasn’t until the Civil Rights Movement that Juneteenth became more widespread. Though the holiday had been celebrated for decades by that point, Detroit officially started celebrating Juneteenth in the 1990s. This year, I will be celebrating by visiting The Charles H. Wright Museum of African American History in Detroit, an extraordinary space and the nation's largest institution dedicated exclusively to African American history and culture. Amidst the celebrations, I hope you’ll join me in taking some time today for reflection and honoring those who fought for Black freedom in America by continuing their fight. It is an important milestone, and a reminder that the fight for justice and equality is never over. Thank you, Elissa PAID FOR BY ELISSA SLOTKIN FOR MICHIGAN P.O. Box 4145 East Lansing, MI 48826

Friend, Today is Juneteenth! More than 160 years since Black Americans won freedom from slavery, the struggle for Black liberation and equity continues. For example, in my majority-Black hometown of Detroit, we’re still fighting against our city’s anti-Black property tax system, which taxes the _least_ expensive homes _six times_ _more_ than the _most_ expensive homes. The wealth gap between Black and white families keeps widening, and our government is still making it worse. On average, Black American homeowners pay 10-13 percent more in property taxes than white homeowners. To correct this injustice, Black-led nonprofit organization Cody Rouge Community Action Alliance helps lower-income residents apply for property tax exemptions and assistance. Cody Rouge Community Action Alliance operates in Far West Detroit’s redlined neighborhoods, keeping families in their homes through safety upgrades, much-needed home repairs, and tools to help seniors age with dignity. Let me tell you a truth that most American history classes will dance around until the bell rings.

In the period after Juneteenth - liberation - 1865 - immediately following the Civil War, **Black men held office**. Not a few. Hundreds. Two Black senators. Fourteen Black congressmen. Hundreds of state legislators, mayors, sheriffs, tax collectors, judges. Hiram Revels. Blanche K. Bruce. Robert Smalls -- an enslaved man during the Civil War who stole a Confederate ship, sailed it to Union lines, and then served five terms in the US House of Representatives.

| [](https://substack.com/redirect/75416519-ee1f-4ef2-a0b8-c696ee677aeb?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---

Schools were built. For the first time in American history, Black children -- children who had been legally forbidden from learning to read -- sat in public school classrooms. The Freedmen's Bureau established over four thousand schools across the South, educating a quarter of a million children and adults.

Wealth was accumulated. Land was redistributed. The promise of forty acres and a mule -- never fully delivered, but delivered enough to terrify the plantation class -- gave formerly enslaved families a toehold on economic independence. Black farmers grew crops, built homes, started businesses, voted in elections, served on juries, wrote constitutions.

**It was called Reconstruction. And it was working.**
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/b2a60ecb-64bc-444f-aebd-dac9528b9935?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
The flag of Juneteenth - a supernova of possibility on a new horizon.
Not perfectly. Not without violence and backlash and the endless, exhausting labor of people who had just been freed from chattel slavery and were expected to build a democracy from scratch with no resources, no protection, and no guarantee that the federal government would not abandon them. But working.
Black literacy rates climbed. Black political participation exploded. Black families built generational wealth for the first time in centuries. Juneteenth marked the beginning of that opportunity to just _start_ to reclaim dignity, put down roots, build, grow, and flourish in freedom.

**And white America dismantled it.**

Not because Reconstruction failed. Because it was working. Because a multiracial democracy in the American South -- Black men voting, Black men holding office, Black children going to school, Black families accumulating land and wealth -- was proof that the entire edifice of white supremacy was a lie. And the people who had built their power on that lie could not tolerate the evidence of their own deception.

So they retaliated. The Ku Klux Klan. The White League. The Red Shirts. Paramilitary terrorist organizations, funded by the former plantation class, armed to the teeth, committed to the violent overthrow of democratically elected governments. They murdered Black politicians in their homes. They massacred entire communities -- Colfax, Louisiana, 1873; Hamburg, South Carolina, 1876; Wilmington, North Carolina, 1898. They burned schools to the ground. They drove Black families off the land they had legally acquired. They stuffed ballot boxes, intimidated voters, assassinated elected officials, and staged coups against legally constituted state governments.

By 1877, the federal government -- exhausted, distracted, and increasingly indifferent to Black suffering -- withdrew the last troops from the South.
**Reconstruction was over. Jim Crow began.**

And here is the part that will make you furious, if you are not already. Racism: The lie that white supremacy told -- the lie that Black people were incapable of self-governance, that Black people were intellectually inferior, that Black people needed to be controlled for their own good -- was not an accident. It was not a natural prejudice. It was not the inevitable product of cultural difference.

It was engineered. Deliberately. As a f'ing PR program.

You want to know when racism was invented? Not prejudice -- that is as old as humanity. But the specific, systematic, pseudo-scientific ideology of white supremacy that was used to justify chattel slavery? That was built in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries by slaveholders who needed to convince poor white people to fight and die for a system that kept them poor too. If poor white people allied with enslaved Black people -- if they recognized their shared exploitation -- the entire system would collapse. So the plantation class invented a story: _you are white, they are Black. You are superior, they are inferior. Your poverty is temporary; their enslavement is eternal. Whatever you do not have, at least you are not them._

That story is still running. Four hundred years later. It has been updated, repackaged, rebranded, and distributed through every medium available -- from the pulpit to the classroom to the television to the algorithm -- but it is the same story. _You are white. They are Black. Your struggles are their fault. Your pain is their doing. Whatever you do not have, at least you are not them._

And it works. It has always worked. That is the tragedy. That is the genius of the thing. The people who engineered white supremacy understood something that their descendants have never forgotten: it is easier to convince a poor white person to hate a Black person than it is to convince them to hate a billionaire. Because the billionaire looks like them. Talks like them. Shares their skin color and their church and their cultural touchstones. The billionaire has the decency to hide. The billionaire pays for the ads that say the problem is immigrants, the problem is welfare queens, the problem is affirmative action, the problem is critical race theory, the problem is anyone except the people actually pulling the levers of power.

So here we are. A similar pattern repeating today. A multiracial coalition -- Black, brown, white, Asian, Indigenous -- won the White House in 2020. Not perfectly. Not without compromise. Not without corruption. But a coalition committed, at least rhetorically, to democracy, to equity, to the proposition that Black lives matter and that the arc of the moral universe bends toward justice.

And the backlash has been ferocious. **Not because that coalition failed.**_**Because it was working.**_ Because the sight of a Black woman running for president, of Black men and women in Congress, of a multiracial working class organizing for better wages and healthcare and housing -- that sight is proof that white supremacy is a lie. And the people who have built their power on that lie cannot tolerate the evidence.

So they have retaliated. Voter suppression laws. Book bans. Gerrymandering the electoral districts. The erasure of Black history from school curricula. The criminalization of protest. The dismantling of voting rights protections. The systematic purging of Black voters from the rolls. The relentless, day-and-night propaganda machine that tells white Americans that they are under attack, that their country is being stolen from them, that the only way to save America is to return to a past that never existed.

This is not new. This is Jim Crow following Reconstruction, run again. We know this script. The same playbook, the same lies, the same terror, the same refusal to accept that a multiracial democracy is possible.

**And we have to get past this. In a big way. If we are going to have any decent future as a country.**

I do not mean forget it. I mean recognize it for what it is -- an engineered, centuries-old PR campaign designed to keep working people fighting each other instead of fighting the people robbing them blind -- and refuse to play along anymore. We need to understand that the only way to break the cycle is to build something that does not depend on anyone being beneath anyone else. We need to do the work, every day, to see the humanity in people who do not look like us, and to demand that they see the humanity in us, and to refuse to let the billionaires and their media apparatus divide us with the same tired lies our great-great-grandparents were sold.

Reconstruction worked. That is why they destroyed it. The multiracial democracy we are trying to build today is working. That is why they are trying to destroy it. The only question is whether we have the courage and power to defend it better than our ancestors did -- to refuse the lie, to cross the color line, to build coalitions that cannot be broken, to love each other enough to fight for a future that belongs to all of us.

My name is Melissa Chaudhry. I am a white woman married to a Asian Muslim man. I have seen racism up close -- in the ICE detention center where a decorated, disabled, American military veteran in wheelchair who's never broken any US laws in 30 years here - was abducted from his citizenship appointment last year and illegally imprisoned and put in solitary confinement under 24/7 bright light, a known form of torture. I fought in four federal courts for justice, up against the US Attorney General with no lawyers, and I won. I see the structural racism in the sheer **existence** of those detention centers - and I see it in the faces of people who look at our family and see something they cannot accept.

And I see racism in my district. In the unequal justice that sentences Black and Brown youth differently from white. In the structural deprivation and economic inequality that cripples the Black, Brown, and immigrant communities of South Seattle, Seatac, Tukwila, and Kent. In the environmental racism that hits the communities surrounding SeaTac airport - all poor, all people of color - with inescapable air pollution from the airplane smog that leads to higher cancer rates, higher stillbirths and miscarriages, and lower test scores just based on where people can afford to live.

I am running for Congress because the people deserve a representative who will tell the truth: that racism was invented by the powerful to keep us divided, that it is still working exactly as designed, and that the only way to win is to refuse to play.

Care. Courage. The Constitution.
**Vote Melissa for Congress.**

Every book PR person thinks it's a good idea -- I question who you think in their audience would buy anything though.
And I also question why we give the far left women of the View the credibility of leaders on our side appear who give them ratings while the openly -- and falsely - lie about our people and policies.
True to character, the hosts tried to ambush the VP on his views of President Trump, the border, and whatever else they could throw at him.
Vance didn't flinch.
He called out years of media lies, defended strong border policies, and explained how we're cleaning up the mess left by the Biden administration.
My favorite moment though, was when Joy Behar pressed him on his past criticism of Trump.
The Vice President responded with something you rarely hear in politics: humility.

A look at the origins of Juneteenth and why its lessons still matter today.
| | [](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/133640713/628568186/-1405467182?nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMDEvMS82MTY0NSIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICJjYTgxMGQwMy1mODZiLWYxMTEtOGZjYi0wMDBkM2ExNGI2ZDYiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=TDaeo4SrlM0XFC9Tx9nXttwdKVEucd8tRNqjx5V6XZI=&emci=02bded2d-1a6b-f111-8fcb-000d3a18905c&emdi=ca810d03-f86b-f111-8fcb-000d3a14b6d6&ceid=14565883)

| | Welcome back to Fact Friday. **Today, we're discussing Juneteenth, a holiday with roots right here in Texas.** While Juneteenth is now legally recognized as a federal holiday, many Americans are still unfamiliar with its origins and why it remains such an important part of our nation's history. So today, let's take a closer look at where Juneteenth comes from, what it commemorates, and why its lessons continue to matter today. The story begins during the Civil War. We all know the headlines, but the reality in Texas looked very different. The Emancipation Proclamation was signed on January 1, 1863, but out here on the frontier, that piece of paper didn't immediately change the lives of enslaved Texans. Because Texas was so isolated from the rest of the country, Union troops weren't here to enforce it. Texas plantation owners deliberately hid the news, keeping thousands of people in bondage for over two and a half years after they were legally free. That changed on June 19, 1865, when Union Major General Gordon Granger arrived in Galveston and announced that enslaved people in Texas were free. Some enslaved Texans already knew that emancipation had been declared, but without the power to enforce it, freedom remained largely out of reach. For thousands of Black Texans, the announcement marked the long-overdue realization of a freedom that had already been legally declared more than two years earlier. The very next year, Black Texans began organizing celebrations to mark June 19. As families moved beyond Texas over the generations, they carried those traditions with them, helping transform a Texas commemoration into a national observance that was ultimately recognized as a federal holiday in 2021. That's why Juneteenth, originating right here in Texas, is a reminder that progress isn't always immediate. Freedom, equality, and justice have always required persistence, sacrifice, and the determination of ordinary people who believed our nation could live up to its highest ideals. As we celebrate Juneteenth this year, we honor the resilience of those who endured slavery, the generations who preserved this history, and the ongoing work of building a country where the promises of liberty and opportunity truly extend to everyone. If you want to keep getting clear, fact-based breakdowns of the issues affecting our community, make sure you stay connected and share this with someone who should be paying attention, too. clean_body: A look at the origins of Juneteenth and why its lessons still matter today. | | | | Welcome back to Fact Friday. Today, we're discussing Juneteenth, a holiday with roots right here in Texas. While Juneteenth is now legally recognized as a federal holiday, many Americans are still unfamiliar with its origins and why it remains such an important part of our nation's history. So today, let's take a closer look at where Juneteenth comes from, what it commemorates, and why its lessons continue to matter today. The story begins during the Civil War. We all know the headlines, but the reality in Texas looked very different. The Emancipation Proclamation was signed on January 1, 1863, but out here on the frontier, that piece of paper didn't immediately change the lives of enslaved Texans. Because Texas was so isolated from the rest of the country, Union troops weren't here to enforce it. Texas plantation owners deliberately hid the news, keeping thousands of people in bondage for over two and a half years after they were legally free. That changed on June 19, 1865, when Union Major General Gordon Granger arrived in Galveston and announced that enslaved people in Texas were free. Some enslaved Texans already knew that emancipation had been declared, but without the power to enforce it, freedom remained largely out of reach. For thousands of Black Texans, the announcement marked the long-overdue realization of a freedom that had already been legally declared more than two years earlier. The very next year, Black Texans began organizing celebrations to mark June 19. As families moved beyond Texas over the generations, they carried those traditions with them, helping transform a Texas commemoration into a national observance that was ultimately recognized as a federal holiday in 2021. That's why Juneteenth, originating right here in Texas, is a reminder that progress isn't always immediate. Freedom, equality, and justice have always required persistence, sacrifice, and the determination of ordinary people who believed our nation could live up to its highest ideals. As we celebrate Juneteenth this year, we honor the resilience of those who endured slavery, the generations who preserved this history, and the ongoing work of building a country where the promises of liberty and opportunity truly extend to everyone. # Celebrating Juneteenth: Honoring a legacy of freedom
---
[|
---](https://jonnyutah4congress.us14.list-manage.com/track/click?u=dc76e2ed74de192812d6308cf&id=7734c5f9a8&e=c29ddb867a)
| | _Photo accredited to_[ _NPS/Terry Adams_](https://jonnyutah4congress.us14.list-manage.com/track/click?u=dc76e2ed74de192812d6308cf&id=1e18ba8faf&e=c29ddb867a) _from the African American Civil War Memorial in Washington, D.C._
---
| | Today, we commemorate the Emancipation Proclamation formally enforced on June 19, 1865 when news reached Galveston, Texas at the end of the Civil War.

[”...all persons held as slaves...are, and henceforth shall be free.”](https://jonnyutah4congress.us14.list-manage.com/track/click?u=dc76e2ed74de192812d6308cf&id=05a16ab829&e=c29ddb867a)

Not only did this declare all enslaved persons free, it allowed Black men to enlist in the Union Army and Navy and actively fight for the end of slavery! African-Americans have fought bravely in every war since the Revolutionary War, even while being denied the very freedoms they were defending.
Today, as we reflect on what our 16th Commander in Chief, President Abraham Lincoln, envisioned for the nation – we remember that true service includes all races and peoples. There is room for everyone.
Thank you for supporting our veterans!
Semper Fi,
-Jonny Larsen
---

As long as we all work together, we will take back Alaska’s U.S. Senate
seat.

The strength of this campaign has always come from regular people stepping
up when it counted. And it means a lot to me that so many of you have
faith in our ability to win. Together, we’re building a movement.

Thanks for being a part of it.

- Mary

name: Dr. Shirley Weber
subject: Freedom finally reached Galveston
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Shirley Weber for Secretary of State 2026
body:
https://drshirleyweber.com/?utm_source=email%20wrapper&utm_medium=email%20wrapper&utm_campaign=email%20wrapper [https://drshirleyweber.com/?utm_source=email%20wrapper&utm_medium=email%20wrapper&utm_campaign=email%20wrapper]
Happy Juneteenth, friends.

161 years ago today, freedom finally reached Galveston Bay.

When union troops read General Granger’s order, a quarter million enslaved Texans learned that the Emancipation Proclamation—signed more than two years earlier—meant they too were free.

Juneteenth is both a celebration and a time for reflection. In it, we see the fulfilment of the American promise for people who never stopped believing that a better future is possible. And a recognition that the battle for justice is never over.

And this Juneteenth arrives at a sobering moment.

In April, Trump’s Supreme Court issued its ruling in Louisiana v. Callais, shredding Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act and dismantling the last fully-functioning federal safeguard against racial discrimination at the polls.

In practice, the Supreme Court has told states can return to the practice of erasing Black political power from their district maps, so long as they label it a partisan strategy.

Make no mistake: The Trump Court is hellbent on rebuilding the legal scaffolding of Jim Crow —repealing the Voting Rights Act one decision at a time and unraveling the hard-fought progress that Black Americans won through over a century of marches, lawsuits, and sacrifices.

For my family and millions of others, it’s wrenching to see the scaffolding dismantled and resurrected in our lifetime. My grandparents spent their lives in the segregated South without ever marking a ballot. My mother and father only voted leaving Arkansas for Los Angeles. Only a single generation separates their disenfranchisement from the office I hold now, where I safeguard the votes of the largest electorate in America.

That’s the arc this Court’s majority is working to reverse. I refuse to sit idly by while it happens.

Here in California, our elections will remain accessible, our vote-by-mail system will remain intact, and any attempt to disenfranchise or intimidate our voters will be met in the courtroom – where we have prevailed before and will again.

The lessons of Juneteenth could not be more relevant in this moment: Liberation can be delayed, obstructed, even hidden from the very people it belongs to – but a community that keeps faith with freedom will see it arrive.

So let’s celebrate today. Rest, rejoice, and honor those who carried us this far.

But tomorrow we organize, because there is too much at stake and too much has been sacrificed to surrender a single inch.

Only when every citizen can vote freely and efforts to marginalize and silence voters of color cease, can we truly be a democracy of the people, by the people, and for the people.

In solidarity,

-Dr. Shirley N. Weber

On this day in 1865, the news of President Lincoln's order of emancipation finally reached enslaved people in Galveston, Texas. It marked a key turning point in our nation's history: the end of slavery in each and every corner of America.
Today, we know this significant day as Juneteenth.
Juneteenth gives us an opportunity to celebrate the countless achievements and contributions that Black Americans have made to Nevada and to our country. It's also an opportunity to reflect on the consequences of this despicable chapter in America's story - and to renew our commitment to fighting the racism, bigotry, and hatred that continues to prevent all Americans from being truly equal to this day.
This year, our shared commitment to this continued fight is as important as it has ever been.
We are currently witnessing freedom and equality under dire threat. To see this threat on full display, look no further than the Supreme Court's recent ruling to gut the Voting Rights Act.
More than half a century ago, the United States enacted this landmark legislation to ensure _all_ Americans have an equal opportunity to participate in our democracy. Now, the six ultraconservative justices have ruled to allow state legislatures to rip this fundamental right away.
Their decision in _Louisiana v. Callais_ will allow Republicans to draw district lines that undercut the political power of millions of Black voters. It's an attack on voting rights - and on our very democracy.
That's why I am calling on you to join me in renewing our resolve in the fight for freedom, for equal opportunity, and for the fundamental rights of every American. We have made incredible progress together, but we still have so much work to do to achieve a truly equitable future. And that future is _always_ worth fighting for.
I'm wishing you a happy Juneteenth. Thank you for standing with me in the fight ahead of us.

| [](https://substack.com/redirect/dfe94a66-459e-418f-95e7-ddf909f2e840?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Source: Department of Justice
Let there be no more arguments about Maine's fentanyl epidemic: The market is run by transnational criminal organizations based in the Dominican Republic.
According to a superseding indictment and a 465-page affidavit filed last week in Massachusetts District Court, the Lawrence, Mass.-based Trinitarios gang ran an elaborate, hierarchical drug-trafficking and firearms-trafficking organization that exploited Maine to sell narcotics and obtain guns.
According to the Department of Justice, the twenty-six alleged leaders, members, and associates of the Trinitarios -- a transnational, Dominican-rooted street gang with a well-known foothold in Mass. -- conspired to run street drugs all over New England.
These 26 bring the grand total of arrests stemming from the long-running organized crime probe to 56, making the enforcement action comparable to any the FBI ever carried out against the infamous Whitey Bulger and the Winter Hill Gang.
The Dominican gangsters are, the DOJ says, tied to five murders and nineteen attempted murders. At least seven of the individuals named in DOJ affidavits and indictments were Dominican illegal aliens.
Lawrence, Haverhill, and Boston play a large role in the narrative, but the affidavit makes clear that Maine is the New England state where Dominican transnational criminals control, run, and profit from the synthetic opiate markets as well as cocaine and methamphetamine.
The gang favored Maine not only for its small per capita number of cops and its drug-addicted customer-base, but also because of the product it could bring back to Massachusetts: guns.
According to the U.S. Attorney's Office in Massachusetts, the sprawling RICO case involved the DOJ's District of Maine, the Maine Attorney General's Office, the Maine State Police, the Maine Drug Enforcement Agency, and several local and county law enforcement agencies in Maine.
The story a Homeland Security Investigations special agent lays out, in the gang's own recorded words, explains exactly how a criminal enterprise headquartered in the Merrimack Valley turned rural Maine into a sales territory.
The document is likely the most detailed look ever provided to the public about the reality of transnational organized criminal groups trafficking fentanyl throughout New England.
It should be required reading for anyone who wants to comment on the opioid epidemic in Maine -- and potential solutions.
[Read: Superseding Indictment Shows Dominican Gangs Run Maine Fentanyl](https://substack.com/redirect/9e39fda5-a27e-4657-97e0-79cb1e0a7a3d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Subscribe to The Robinson Report for New England news...
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack..52XVR9O5f1vpTeP81UisyF8VTptae0c5e3v9kTaBUB4?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget-preamble&utm_content=202631996)
## "Stop the pipeline of drugs heading north"
Prosecutors say the Massachusetts "State Supreme" -- the gang's top in-state authority -- is responsible not only for the chapters in Massachusetts and the Manchester, New Hampshire chapter, but also for the Trinitarios operating in Maine, "where the gang operates a lucrative drug trade."
The investigation is called Operation Paper Machetes. Phase one, "Lime-Light," took down the Lynn chapter in February 2025. Phase two, "Never-Green," is the one unsealed this month. According to the affidavit, one of its four stated goals was to "stop the pipeline of drugs heading north and firearms coming south."
The structure makes Maine not just a place to find drug-addicted customers, but a destination for murderous illegal alien gang bangers to get their hands on firearms.
The clearest window into how it worked comes from Yordali Yorro -- "OG Low," the alleged leader of the Lawrence chapter, whom investigators assess was effectively running the whole Massachusetts operation after the 2025 arrests.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/c9390989-c19b-403a-9145-d586b8888a02?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Yorro is described as a Puerto Rican-born U.S. citizen.
The affidavit includes a transcript from a 2024 recording literally called "Recording of Trip to Bring Drugs to Maine" in which Yorro narrates the business model with the casual fluency of a man describing his commute.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/d15d0c52-fce3-47b8-a521-748809f33c24?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
At one point in the transcript, Yorro describes the free and easy life his employees in Maine have while they sling deadly narcotics throughout the state -- a problem he characterizes as a corporate leadership issue. He then explains the cold economics of dealing drugs in Vacationland.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/d108702c-7720-442d-a865-188e74154dbb?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/8d5aa24c-f16a-4ac7-86fd-efb9b15d8421?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/115927c9-51ba-453e-9c38-967fc1e6d42a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Yorro talks about buying "work" and bringing it "up here." He prices cocaine at $125 a gram for the Maine buyer -- well above Massachusetts street rates -- and walks through cooking it into crack to squeeze roughly $3,100 out of a single ounce. He describes setting up two associates in a Maine trap house to move product, and complains that the pair burned through the equivalent of more than a hundred grams of fentanyl in DoorDash and PlayStation time while they sat around being bored. He calls Maine "hunting ground." He muses about how cheap guns are up here -- a .22 for $320, AR-platform rifles for $500 or $600 -- and recounts how a couple of his contacts broke into a gun store and made off with 64 firearms.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/b5f1c2f6-2dd6-454b-8601-3c299584689f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|

---|---|---
The senior member James Cabrera -- "Trensita" -- fills in the logistics.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/965ae52a-942c-497d-a0cc-cc25d5f72983?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|

| [](https://substack.com/redirect/b0c07997-4786-44c9-9299-d09e57db751d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
In recordings the affidavit ties explicitly to Maine drug trafficking, Cabrera describes hauling a kilogram and a half of cocaine and some 700 grams of fentanyl north on a single run, and using unlicensed runners for the five-and-a-half-hour drive.
One runner, "Joppy," made the round trip alone in a rental car with no license, drove roughly eleven or twelve hours in a night, and got paid $1,000. Cabrera's own stated plan: send eight ounces up at a time and "head up north, speed limit" the whole way. It is the freight operation of a man who has done the math on rural interstate enforcement and likes his odds.
Jervis Almanzar, "JB," a Lawrence chapter member born in 2004, was charged in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maine back in December 2023. He pleaded guilty in August 2024 to two counts of distributing 40 grams or more of fentanyl, and in January 2025 he was sentenced to 60 months in federal prison, where he sits now.
According to the court record in that case, Almanzar sold a cooperating witness in Maine roughly 300 grams of fentanyl.

## A trap house in Piscataquis, a shooting in Paris, a police incident in Rumford
The Piscataquis County Sheriff's Department got a thank-you in the DOJ press release for a reason. The affidavit references a separate federal case, _United States v. Puello & Jenkins_, built around drugs and two firearms recovered from a trap house in Maine.
Xavier Puello -- "Bodega," another charged Lawrence member -- is named in both that case and this month's superseding indictment, with a dedicated section of the affidavit devoted to his drug distribution in Maine in the spring of 2025.
The gangsters fingered in the latest indictments are also directly tied to gun violence cases in Maine.
The affidavit contains another section on an April 16, 2025 shooting in Paris, Maine, and another on an August 15, 2025 police shooting in Rumford, Maine -- the latter including a recording in which the Boston chapter's alleged leader, Luis Cabral, is said to confess to the incident, along with recordings of fellow Boston member Martin Taveras.
## The bigger picture
The affidavit traces the Trinitarios to the New York prison system of the 1990s, organized around Dominican identity, a written "Magna Carta," lime-green colors, crossed-machete iconography, and the slogan _Dios, Patria, Libertad_. Prosecutors describe a recruiting operation aimed at juveniles in Lawrence and Lynn high schools, with initiation "missions" that amount to shootings and beatings, and a habit of advertising the whole enterprise in music videos full of guns, cash, and gang regalia.
What this month's filing establishes is that the organization's reach didn't stop at the greater Boston area. It ran a managed drug economy into Maine, armed itself partly out of Maine, and left behind a wake of gun violence and Mainers addicted to narcotics.

| | [](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/133644536/628579176/372983947?refcode=MW_ATA_EM_FR_WhyImRunning_260619_T1_1&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQNDAvMS84ODY1NCIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICJkMzM4ZWYzMy1mYzZiLWYxMTEtOGZjYi0wMDBkM2ExNGI2ZDYiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=tu3e17goQkzKBAdF281fem7WTTomLD7UEbRNoIEGlvk=) Derek –

This is a longer email than I normally send, because I need to share with you directly about why I decided to run for reelection.

If you’re already with me in the fight to stop President Trump’s dangerous agenda – and get something done to make life easier for working families – then I am asking you to chip in today to help me win this critical US Senate race:

[_**https://secure.actblue.com/donate/mw-email-260601-goal**_](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/133644537/628579177/-1133191615?refcode=MW_ATA_EM_FR_WhyImRunning_260619_T1_1&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQNDAvMS84ODY1NCIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICJkMzM4ZWYzMy1mYzZiLWYxMTEtOGZjYi0wMDBkM2ExNGI2ZDYiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=tu3e17goQkzKBAdF281fem7WTTomLD7UEbRNoIEGlvk=)

As Virginians struggle with the rising cost of health care, gas, groceries, and housing, we’ve seen President Trump’s priorities:
* A monument blocking Arlington National Cemetery.
* Renaming buildings and airports after himself.
* A 1.8 billion dollar slush fund for his allies who attacked the Capitol on January 6th.
* And even a proposal for a $250 bill with Trump’s face on it.

**If this White House put even half as much energy into working to lower costs as it does into stoking the president’s ego, American families wouldn’t need that new $250 bill just to fill up their gas tanks.**

To me, this fight is personal. Like so many others, I grew up in a middle-class family, and I was the first in my family to graduate from college.

Early in my career, I decided to go into business. I took my lifesavings, about $5,000, and invested into a start-up. The company went broke in about six weeks. My second business venture failed in about six months, but the remarkable thing about this country is, I got a third shot. I was fortunate to get into the cell phone business and founded a leading telecommunications company, which would eventually become Nextel.

I got into politics because I believe that everyone in this country should get the same fair shot at success that I had. That’s what this campaign is about.

**And that’s why I am so damn frustrated that every action President Trump has taken in office is fundamentally making it harder for Virginians to make ends meet, let alone try to get ahead. **

# [](https://act.sarahmcbride.com/go/1269?t=1&akid=3439%2E21716%2EXsuAow)
Today is Juneteenth, friends.
Juneteenth is more than a holiday — it’s a call to action.
On this day in 1865, Union soldiers arrived at the last stronghold of the Confederacy with the news that President Lincoln had decreed all enslaved African Americans to be free.
While the Emancipation Proclamation technically went into effect in 1863, it took more than two years for the news to reach all parts of the country.
Today, as we mark the end of slavery and celebrate our nation’s diversity, let us remember that freedom will find a way — but only if we work for it, fight for it, and continuously recommit ourselves to it.
Happy Juneteenth,
Sarah McBride

# [A Father's Day Reflection on My Two Jack Murphys](https://substack.com/app-link/post?publication_id=4399133&post_id=202733266&utm_source=post-email-title&utm_campaign=email-post-title&isFreemail=true&r=1hvr60&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjo5MDUwMTE5MiwicG9zdF9pZCI6MjAyNzMzMjY2LCJpYXQiOjE3ODE4ODc1NzcsImV4cCI6MTc4NDQ3OTU3NywiaXNzIjoicHViLTQzOTkxMzMiLCJzdWIiOiJwb3N0LXJlYWN0aW9uIn0.nYvk8WO1GxdjO2i333CwJ7ncpa9YOiHN2QRrmnLQMeA)
### On showing up and being present.
| | [Patrick J. Murphy](https://substack.com/@patrickmurphypa)
---
| Jun 19
---
| [](https://substack.com/@patrickmurphypa)
---

---
| | | [](https://substack.com/app-link/post?publication_id=4399133&post_id=202733266&utm_source=substack&isFreemail=true&submitLike=true&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjo5MDUwMTE5MiwicG9zdF9pZCI6MjAyNzMzMjY2LCJyZWFjdGlvbiI6IuKdpCIsImlhdCI6MTc4MTg4NzU3NywiZXhwIjoxNzg0NDc5NTc3LCJpc3MiOiJwdWItNDM5OTEzMyIsInN1YiI6InJlYWN0aW9uIn0.s0AKnj5nT8ron13xacE8crYanZzz4qCYL3RFwmm6e68&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=email-reaction&r=1hvr60)

---

My father never said much about what made a man.
He didn't have to. Jack Murphy grew up in a trailer park in National Park, New Jersey, the son of a World War II Navy veteran who came home from the Pacific and, like many men of his generation, got on with life. My Pop-Pop drove a tractor trailer for Teamsters Local 107 and somehow still found time to serve as commander of the local VFW post. In our family, that wasn't considered remarkable. It was simply what grown men did.
My father followed a similar path. He enlisted in the Navy straight out of high school during Vietnam through the Buddy Program with his cousin, Johnny Kelly. After his service, he came home, joined the Philadelphia Police Department, married my mother, and raised a family in a rowhouse in Northeast Philly.
He had tattoos up both arms and a short fuse that surfaced whenever he spotted an injustice. It didn't matter whether it was a reckless driver, a neighborhood bully, or an umpire blowing a call against his beloved Phillies. Before he and my mother were married, he saw a trucker catcalling and honking at her outside her bank job in center city as she was walking out of work, ran through rush hour traffic, pulled the driver through the window, and punched him in the nose. There's a reason Murphy is an old Irish word for sea warrior.
Some of my clearest memories of my father are from the front seat of his car at 5 a.m., driving to hockey practice while the rest of Philadelphia was still asleep. There were summer weekends at Single-A baseball games, my father coaching third base in oppressive heat as if the World Series depended on it. He worked three jobs into his late sixties and retired with two pensions. I never heard him once complain.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/aa3fd0c3-1e44-4ebd-90f6-b398510ac40f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
The first time I ever saw him cry was at Pop-Pop's funeral when I was in the third grade. He pulled a white handkerchief from his pocket, brushed it against the corner of his eye, and tucked it back away.
The biggest lesson I took from my father was the power of showing up. So I built my life around it.
I carried it to Baghdad with the 82nd Airborne. I carried it to Congress and later to the Pentagon. And I carried it into fatherhood, where I coached my son Jack's teams, drove him to practices, and showed up for every game and family dinner I could. Even when I was running the Army from Washington during the week, I was home most weekends coaching. I was there. Ninety percent, every time, the same way my father had been there for me. What took me far too long to understand is that showing up and being present are not always the same thing.
You can be at every game and still be somewhere else. You can show up in every room and still leave the most important things unsaid. You can keep moving and call it strength when really it's just motion. What works in a combat zone or on a campaign doesn't necessarily work when your son just needs you to sit down and be uncertain or vulnerable alongside him.
My son Jack's never gotten himself into real trouble. He's just done what sixteen-year-olds do.
Assignments slipped through the cracks. Sometimes he was late for school or church. Sometimes he'd disappear into his room instead of joining the rest of us downstairs.
And over time I realized the issue wasn't just what he was doing. It was what I wasn't doing. A few months ago, I sat down with him and had a conversation I should have had much sooner. That conversation was the hardest thing I've ever done. Harder than Baghdad. Harder than any vote I cast in Congress and I cast some that cost me everything politically. Because in Baghdad and in Congress I always knew what I stood for and what it took to win. In that conversation with my son, I had to face what I had spent years avoiding.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/b9a9f78a-c84c-40bc-9120-461b6e3ce996?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
The boundaries I hadn't drawn. The things I hadn't said. The silence that was mine. Eight pages written out that I sat with him as he read it. No more silent agreements of looking the other way.
I did not get here alone. And I am not good at this yet. I want to be clear about that -- there is no clean resolution here, no morning I woke up transformed. Holding the boundaries takes practice. I am practicing.
But I know what I'm practicing for.
I want my son to thrive. I want him to walk into a room with confidence. To have a voice and know when to use it. To be capable, dependable, and comfortable in his own skin. To be the kind of man who leaves people better than he found them and makes the world around him a little better too. Those things don't happen by accident. Someone has to model them. I can't give him what he needs if I don't show him what vulnerability looks like.
I was anxious about sharing my expectations with him. I love him so much, I was afraid it wouldn't go well. I'm showing him now--imperfectly, out loud, where he can see me doing the work. Letting him see me try, stumble, and keep going has made all the difference. Our relationship over the last two months has gotten so much better. He earned his license and made the honor roll for only the second time.
My father, Jack Murphy, taught me that 90% of success is showing up.
My son Jack Murphy is teaching me about the other 10%.
Pop-Pop came home from the Pacific and showed my father what duty looked like. My father showed me what it meant to be there, no matter what. And now my son--sixteen years old, working at the Jersey Shore this summer, carrying the same name across four generations of Murphy men--is teaching me something we never talked much about.
That strength isn't just showing up. It's being present.
That is the lesson I'm carrying with me this Father's Day. Not the 90% I inherited. The 10% I am still earning.
Happy Father's Day to my two Jack Murphys. I love you more than you'll ever know.

Lately, it's easy to feel discouraged by what we're seeing in the world around us, but here's something I believe with everything I have: **People get stronger when they come together in difficult times and refuse to let those challenges define what 's possible.**
Not just on Election Day. Every day. In town halls and diners and community events. In conversations that don't make the news. In the quiet, unglamorous work of building a campaign from the ground up because you believe the people of your district deserve better than what they've been getting.

This campaign has been built dollar by dollar, conversation by conversation, county by county. No corporate shortcuts or PAC money smoothing the path. Just Americans who are tired of watching their government work for everyone except them deciding to do something about it.
You don't have to live in Tennessee to be part of this fight. When a grassroots campaign beats a 14-year incumbent backed by corporate money, it proves something the establishment desperately doesn't want proven: that the people can still win.

body:
| | | In May, the conservative fake-news outlet the Daily Wire suggested there was Medicaid fraud in Ohio’s home care system. **If there is widespread Medicaid and Medicare fraud, it’s because the system undervalues and underpays these workers and never truly cares about those receiving the care.** But of course, the Trump administration and Republican governors across the country are tightening restrictions on who receives Medicaid-funded home care and who can provide that care, all in the name of **_accountability_**. The real crisis around home-care is that there simply aren’t enough home-care providers. **These aides simply aren’t paid enough for the essential work they provide, so there are very few providers in rural states like Ohio.** Previous rules attempted to solve this problem by paying parents and relatives of those with disabilities to provide care, but Trump and Republican allies are trying to shut that down as well. This is cruelty from politicians to deflect from actual drains on our tax dollars, such as the Iran War and the endless White House renovations. It’s incredibly easy for Republicans to throw disabled people under the bus rather than stand up to Trump and his bullsh*t. **This issue is especially personal for me because I receive in-home care, and I’ve heard the horror stories of those who could no longer afford home care and had to go to an assisted living facility.** Inpatient state-run facilities are often overworked and understaffed. Patients have reported being neglected and assaulted by staff. On top of that, we have a nationwide provider shortage and federal government cuts to Medicaid funding that are going to be felt soon. **Are you exhausted reading this? Because trust me, it’s**** _1000x_****more exhausting living this.** Disability advocates are trying so hard to talk to the Republicans in power, but it’s much easier to ignore a population with very little political power. **That’s why Able Dems is building that political power.** My organization is committed to electing champions and allies of the disabled community to help solve the real Medicaid crisis, not cry foul and pad their own pockets.**** **[I would be so incredibly grateful if you’d donate whatever you can to help fund our advertising and organizing efforts to elect leaders who would protect the disabled community rather than throw them under the bus.](https://click.actionnetwork.org/ss/c/u001.iIBo0N5fSFzEFL40Tn-vtbMETCUYClkOrOh9-SNJfqtHtWNDtXR0WReOmqZcCOXO2FiuxEhBk3zsUTCYW6F8lB7-RffhngK16Xoh7-Vi8mCt6gt3nev0IDvPxYqGlK4P24QsgmVAMhGXEWSqUv8Zx8XGgsp4Fc4vwO5CLGIl27fVGnIRQ-YAQEnqZ2vB3T_R5A_5OKvFfk1C_JIn6qjLnQOBqlioIqHob4kLafkakTgamBo6Hec5FKsSrum2yOoAHWLgQkFG7aK67_aQMl2yu0IXv_gSqHa3oc9BRp6ZSxx2lv4ZbzI3haeRF_M8lTLrWPRW0YsmUXyJMFuQtNTkeuxmg3mBa7YXJXWjfTBj3kh5V1vATqtFyRXl8F8oP2F6AHgV21cOMYwbr5eEQnGWsV0xDq1ItZBfYx-xLegwd50/4rm/_Tltko24SOC5cyaRe99EAw/h0/h001.k6UhXs11c4dSNvWO8rltLwZLUZ81ZRZXIifgdItl8gA)** _If you've saved your payment information with ActBlue Express, your donation will go through immediately._ [Donate $10

clean_body: | | | In May, the conservative fake-news outlet the Daily Wire suggested there was Medicaid fraud in Ohio’s home care system. If there is widespread Medicaid and Medicare fraud, it’s because the system undervalues and underpays these workers and never truly cares about those receiving the care. But of course, the Trump administration and Republican governors across the country are tightening restrictions on who receives Medicaid-funded home care and who can provide that care, all in the name of accountability. The real crisis around home-care is that there simply aren’t enough home-care providers. These aides simply aren’t paid enough for the essential work they provide, so there are very few providers in rural states like Ohio. Previous rules attempted to solve this problem by paying parents and relatives of those with disabilities to provide care, but Trump and Republican allies are trying to shut that down as well. This is cruelty from politicians to deflect from actual drains on our tax dollars, such as the Iran War and the endless White House renovations. It’s incredibly easy for Republicans to throw disabled people under the bus rather than stand up to Trump and his bullsht. This issue is especially personal for me because I receive in-home care, and I’ve heard the horror stories of those who could no longer afford home care and had to go to an assisted living facility. Inpatient state-run facilities are often overworked and understaffed. Patients have reported being neglected and assaulted by staff. On top of that, we have a nationwide provider shortage and federal government cuts to Medicaid funding that are going to be felt soon. Are you exhausted reading this? Because trust me, it’s** 1000xmore exhausting living this. Disability advocates are trying so hard to talk to the Republicans in power, but it’s much easier to ignore a population with very little political power. That’s why Able Dems is building that political power. My organization is committed to electing champions and allies of the disabled community to help solve the real Medicaid crisis, not cry foul and pad their own pockets.** ** If you've saved your payment information with ActBlue Express, your donation will go through immediately. — Able Dems | elects Democrats with disabilities. ## Stars, Speeches, and an $850 Million Price Tag: The Obama Center Opens
Chicago's South Side hosted a Hollywood-grade spectacle Thursday as the $850 million Barack Obama Presidential Center held its dedication, drawing Oprah Winfrey, Steven Spielberg, Tom Hanks, and Bruce Springsteen to Jackson Park.What to Know
* ▸ Four living former presidents attended; the one living president who didn't was Trump. The musical lineup ran from Stevie Wonder to Bono.
* ▸ The museum tower — its design meant to evoke four hands joined in solidarity — is wrapped with an excerpt from Obama's 2015 Selma speech.
* ▸ The Foundation billed the project as an "economic engine for South Side residents," yet locals voice fears of being priced out, and some subcontractors say they still haven't been paid.

The PerspectiveThere's nothing wrong with a president getting a library — every modern one does. But $850 million later, the gap between the celebrity glitz on stage and the neighborhood just past the security perimeter is hard to miss. The South Side was promised an economic engine; what it has, for now, is a monument. Whether the museum changes a single life around it is the question the stars flew home without answering.Read the full story at [Fox News](https://link.mail.beehiiv.com/v1/c/yENOisX%2BZBHN4waAmAE7BV80oTvqxch%2B%2BriwBO8Enj%2Bfx8u6X%2BzwMfTko%2BOq%0AoLxWit01CaLXeEuREVS0tdHZIgmmRz%2FOSjsJMCkYPOQKINn8QlM6amN9qxWT%0AkZsRPhe3i7nh1B2xT%2BPEvYD1HU5uO2F74QowytMRZZRLxjtheIjx3knThbLO%0Ax7ZGzh2MuFtMWCwJFBDb1pwmkg3%2BNjnobQ%3D%3D%0A/42e4088ccc87b8bf).
* * *
★ The Border
## "Alligator Alcatraz" Goes Quiet as Hurricane Season Opens
The Department of Homeland Security says every detainee has now been moved out of the Florida Everglades facility dubbed "Alligator Alcatraz," citing the start of hurricane season — right as Tropical Storm Arthur became the season's first named storm.The Details
* ▸ DHS didn't say how many were transferred or where, or whether the state-run site is closing for good or just riding out the season.
* ▸ Stood up by Gov. Ron DeSantis on a remote airstrip in a matter of days, the facility opened in July 2025 and was built to hold up to **3,000**.
* ▸ "For the safety of the illegal alien detainees, we transferred them," a department spokesperson said.

The PerspectiveThe same critics who spent a year calling this site inhumane now call its emptying a sinister cover story. It can't be both a death trap and a place they're outraged to see cleared out ahead of the storms. Whatever becomes of the tents in the swamp, the bigger point holds: when Washington spent years looking away on the border, states like Florida stepped up.Read the full story at [the Associated Press](https://link.mail.beehiiv.com/v1/c/4rw4d5Iud%2FBC2KzHT%2BO6wtiXlit4nL2ntOJa6WBOMZH3EHplBkSQhAwy0Ozs%0ADyGCcXgQosQBhVh35u77sHq0D5S%2BxVGmhqvEN1wD5EzjCmm4I6Qx4RKzWIil%0AzVAAY1uFm5zLZ5QSWei8seVVY8XxN%2BvWcCpGWSbx6NqoOZtjqo8I0Q4Anja6%0AKgV6A1m8xlohmRSPzfNqmzi3%2F%2Bl9GGhKOg%3D%3D%0A/aa4cc2a60ecb6486).
* * *
★ The World Stage
## The Hard Part: Lebanon Flares as the Iran Talks Slip
The day-old framework is already being tested. After four Israeli soldiers were killed in southern Lebanon, the IDF says it struck more than 80 Hezbollah targets — including command centers in the Bekaa Valley — and the first U.S.–Iran negotiating session in Switzerland was postponed, with Vice President JD Vance scrapping his trip.On the Ground
* ▸ A senior U.S. official said a fresh Israel–Hezbollah ceasefire took effect Friday afternoon, though a Hezbollah spokesperson said the group didn't yet consider it in force.
* ▸ Hezbollah said it would honor the truce if Israel does, but "reserves the right to respond" to any violation.
* ▸ Trump pushed back on claims Iran came out ahead, arguing the campaign — Operation Epic Fury — left the regime in Tehran diminished.

The PerspectiveThis is the hard part of any deal — the day after. A signature at Versailles doesn't disarm Hezbollah, and the proxy fight in Lebanon is exactly where "all fronts" gets tested. The broader framework is holding for now; the brushfire in the south is the thing to watch. We'll keep it clear-eyed — without the pom-poms.Read the full story at [Fox News](https://link.mail.beehiiv.com/v1/c/xHht5gSkyhGVlKwUJqr0S7UX8seButHX74H4%2FXR6wAUOkKoclmC8TSqTXxFJ%0A4LL5oZncaJ8i1TbinDxTdL%2FBrOGP0QMB%2BBvoluuBhR0TvHB8Pc6BWmcA59I8%0A5yBPUsKTc8Sp9q97ihAoaYb3kkvxQT7Fxejg3XawRC5dZvs6LTRzNZO5w0tL%0ANDcfejDFQrKJyVHgEqWOffXNSYoPJ8p6jg%3D%3D%0A/1cce72085de8bf00).
* * *
★ Campaign Trail
## A Split Decision in Georgia Sets Up a Marquee Senate Fight
Georgia's Republican runoffs delivered a mixed verdict this week. Voters handed the Senate nomination to Trump-endorsed Rep. Mike Collins, who will challenge Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff in November — but rejected the president's pick for governor, choosing self-funding businessman Rick Jackson over Lt. Gov. Burt Jones.The Takeaways
* ▸ Collins vs. Ossoff is shaping up as one of the most expensive, most-watched Senate races on the 2026 map — with control of the chamber potentially in the balance.
* ▸ Jackson, who poured roughly $100 million of his own money into the race, will face Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former Atlanta mayor.
* ▸ The night underscored the running tug-of-war between President Trump and popular outgoing Gov. Brian Kemp over the party's direction.

The PerspectiveHere's the straight read: it was an uneven night for the president's endorsement record, and pretending otherwise would be exactly the kind of spin this newsletter exists to cut through. Collins is a strong nominee and the Ossoff seat is winnable. But Georgia Republicans also showed they'll think for themselves — and that's not a weakness in a party, it's a sign of life.Read the full story at [Fox News](https://link.mail.beehiiv.com/v1/c/uRuylhQN757NFwoRTO9WEt3nsOh1MdP8JGkkp1HeQmYTPhcct5bWGaAL2bDE%0A53zcsywQcv0iunfcB0O8XM0vgAxAfQG8PS0kxeTMpr5y0xsNA6fRmhwQKqzz%0AKVqCYK29jtIysklbVkmMXReLfvrxOE9uHtTqYBV9hlv08J6NeFmUaVbZw6eY%0A8EcBIiPj2kJoLNYcT6O7OlbxnS5vUFt5Kg%3D%3D%0A/dbad95083b71aae1).⚡ The Bottom LineFrom a celebrity-studded monument on the South Side to emptied tents in the Everglades, the day was a study in contrasts — the political class celebrating itself while the unglamorous work of security and enforcement carries on. Abroad, a fragile deal faces its first real test in Lebanon; at home, Georgia voters reminded both parties who's actually in charge. We call it as we see it, win or lose. **The truth doesn't take sides — and neither do we.** That's just the truth."The truth isn't conservative or liberal. Ron DeSantis on a remote airstrip in a matter of days, the facility opened in July 2025 and was built to hold up to 3,000. ▸ "For the safety of the illegal alien detainees, we transferred them," a department spokesperson said. The PerspectiveThe same critics who spent a year calling this site inhumane now call its emptying a sinister cover story. It can't be both a death trap and a place they're outraged to see cleared out ahead of the storms. Whatever becomes of the tents in the swamp, the bigger point holds: when Washington spent years looking away on the border, states like Florida stepped up.Read the full story at . ★ The World Stage The Hard Part: Lebanon Flares as the Iran Talks Slip The day-old framework is already being tested. After four Israeli soldiers were killed in southern Lebanon, the IDF says it struck more than 80 Hezbollah targets — including command centers in the Bekaa Valley — and the first U.S.–Iran negotiating session in Switzerland was postponed, with Vice President JD Vance scrapping his trip.On the Ground ▸ A senior U.S. official said a fresh Israel–Hezbollah ceasefire took effect Friday afternoon, though a Hezbollah spokesperson said the group didn't yet consider it in force. ▸ Hezbollah said it would honor the truce if Israel does, but "reserves the right to respond" to any violation. ▸ Trump pushed back on claims Iran came out ahead, arguing the campaign — Operation Epic Fury — left the regime in Tehran diminished. The PerspectiveThis is the hard part of any deal — the day after. A signature at Versailles doesn't disarm Hezbollah, and the proxy fight in Lebanon is exactly where "all fronts" gets tested. The broader framework is holding for now; the brushfire in the south is the thing to watch. We'll keep it clear-eyed — without the pom-poms.Read the full story at . ★ Campaign Trail A Split Decision in Georgia Sets Up a Marquee Senate Fight Georgia's Republican runoffs delivered a mixed verdict this week. Voters handed the Senate nomination to Trump-endorsed Rep. Mike Collins, who will challenge Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff in November — but rejected the president's pick for governor, choosing self-funding businessman Rick Jackson over Lt. Gov. Burt Jones.The Takeaways ▸ Collins vs. Ossoff is shaping up as one of the most expensive, most-watched Senate races on the 2026 map — with control of the chamber potentially in the balance. ▸ Jackson, who poured roughly $100 million of his own money into the race, will face Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former Atlanta mayor. ▸ The night underscored the running tug-of-war between President Trump and popular outgoing Gov. Brian Kemp over the party's direction. The PerspectiveHere's the straight read: it was an uneven night for the president's endorsement record, and pretending otherwise would be exactly the kind of spin this newsletter exists to cut through. Collins is a strong nominee and the Ossoff seat is winnable. But Georgia Republicans also showed they'll think for themselves — and that's not a weakness in a party, it's a sign of life.Read the full story at .⚡ The Bottom LineFrom a celebrity-studded monument on the South Side to emptied tents in the Everglades, the day was a study in contrasts — the political class celebrating itself while the unglamorous work of security and enforcement carries on. Abroad, a fragile deal faces its first real test in Lebanon; at home, Georgia voters reminded both parties who's actually in charge. We call it as we see it, win or lose. The truth doesn't take sides — and neither do we.** That's just the truth."The truth isn't conservative or liberal. It's just the truth."This newsletter presents news from a conservative perspective. subject: Happy Juneteenth

body:

Friend,

Today on Juneteenth, we honor the strength, resilience, and joy of Black communities and celebrate the legacy of liberation. As we do, we must also reflect on race and inequality and continue the work of building a more just and equitable future in New Mexico and beyond for everyone.

As much as this administration wants to, we _cannot_ erase the past and rewrite history; we must take the time to think about the work that still needs to be done to confront the lasting impacts of slavery and racism and ensure every community has the opportunity to thrive.

It is why when I led the Department of the Interior, I fought to invest in historically underserved communities to deliver on a vision of a more equitable America. My work led to the Emmett Till and Mamie Till-Mobley National Monument designation.

And it’s why I’m running for Governor: To fight for every New Mexican. I want to create good-paying jobs, give New Mexicans a raise, and make sure our state is one where everyone has the opportunity to succeed. _Together, we can build a New Mexico that supports every community and gives every person the chance to thrive._
So this Juneteenth, let’s honor those who came before us and recommit to building a better future for every New Mexican, together.
Thank you, and Be Fierce,

Deb

Competitive Analysis Cook Political Report rates this a toss-up. Aaron and MAGA Gov. Joe Lombardo are statistically tied in the polls. All the data boils down to one thing: This race is one of the Democratic Party’s best opportunities to flip a governor’s seat blue. Opposition Overview MAGA Gov. Joe Lombardo has corporate special interest money and the full weight of an incumbent's operation behind him. Outside Republican spending is expected to increase as we head into the fall. This will be one of the most competitive — and expensive — governor's races in the country. Our Path to Victory Aaron's track record as Nevada’s Attorney General uniquely positions him to motivate voters across Nevada who are dissatisfied with the Lombardo-Trump economy. Amplifying his accomplishments will be key to building a broad, winning coalition of voters. Running ads early and launching a comprehensive organizing program is crucially important. We need to build our general election war chest now, while momentum is with us. Every dollar raised in the days after a primary sends a signal that a campaign is strong and ready for the fight ahead. Now that you know exactly what’s at stake and how we can win, can we count on your support? Thank you, Team Ford

Because He Has No Clue What He's Doing](https://default.salsalabs.org/T6713001c-a818-4460-967a-b8d26ae0de8b/368d17ff-e836-4168-8049-c5f0900fbbf9)** The Lincoln Memorial is one of the most iconic and photographed bodies of water in America. It was the site of MLK’s “I Have a Dream” speech, countless other gatherings through the years, and millions if not billions of quiet, reflective moments for visitors from throughout the world. [**But Donald Trump decided it needed an “extreme makeover”, and not surprisingly, he f***ed it up:**](https://default.salsalabs.org/Tc44c8325-0685-414c-95da-7c2df3a12dec/368d17ff-e836-4168-8049-c5f0900fbbf9) The National Park Service had received bids to try again with a total renovation of the granite and grouting. But that could have cost hundreds of millions, Trump said earlier this spring. His solution was to use swimming pool contractors to coat the granite with a spray-on liner, saying the total cost would be between $1.5 million and $2 million. That cost later ballooned to $14.5 million, according to federal records. He hired a company that had fixed swimming pools at Mar-a-Lago without bothering to get bids from other ones (as the law requires). The company apparently had no clue what it was doing, and turned the pool into a massive algae orgy — a sea of green muck. Like Jolly Green Giant Chunky Soup. [**It's going to cost a fortune to fix it, and there's know way the rest of us should pay for his stupidity.**](https://default.salsalabs.org/Ta456d6a2-ed02-4dd8-b79b-75867dffab1d/368d17ff-e836-4168-8049-c5f0900fbbf9) [**Trump needs to fix it and he needs to pay for it from his own funds. Add your name, and demand Trump pay for the repairs.**](https://default.salsalabs.org/T1d1081f7-49e3-4f01-9ca3-a209501755a5/368d17ff-e836-4168-8049-c5f0900fbbf9)

| | Lifе and death Son of Mykhailo Sulyma, Ivan came from a petty noble (szlachta) family. He was born in Rohoshchi (next to Chernihiv). He served as an estate overseer for Stanisław Żółkiewski and later the family of Daniłowicze who inherited his lands; for that service in 1620 he was awarded three villages: Sulimówka, Kuczakiw and Lebedyn. Аll the villages todаy belong to the Boryspil Raion, Kyiv Oblast. His sons included Stepan (died 1659), a captain of Boryspil company, and Fedir (died 1691), a colonel of Pereiaslav regiment. He became popular among the unregistered Cossacks, leading them on campaigns to plunder Crimea and other Ottoman vassal territories. For organizing a revolt on an Ottoman slave galley and freeing Christian slaves[1] he received a medal from Pope Paul V himself. Eventually, Sulyma reached the rank of the hetman, which he held from 1628 to 1629 and 1630 to 1635. In 1635, after returning from an expedition to Black Sea against the Ottomans, he decided to rebel against the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which at that time controlled most of the Cossack territories, and whose nobility was trying to turn militant Cossacks into serfs.[citation needed] Ivan Sulyma took part in numerous campaigns of Sagaidachny against Tatars and Turks. In particular, it was the famous capture of Kafa (modern Theodosia), the main center of the slave trade on the Black Sea, Trapezont, Izmail, and also two attacks on Tsaregrad. On the night of 3 to 4 August 1635 he took the newly constructed Kodak fortress by surprise, burning it and executing its crew of about 200 people under Jean Marion. Egyptian hieroglyphs were the formal writing system used in Ancient Egypt for writing the Egyptian language. Hieroglyphs combined logographic, syllabic and alphabetic elements, with some 1,000 distinct characters.[3][4] Cursive hieroglyphs were used for religious literature on papyrus and wood. The later hieratic and demotic Egyptian scripts were derived from hieroglyphic writing, as was the Proto-Sinaitic script that later evolved into the Phoenician alphabet.[5] Through the Phoenician alphabet's major child systems (the Greek and Aramaic scripts), the Egyptian hieroglyphic script is ancestral to the majority of scripts in modern use, most prominently the Latin and Cyrillic scripts (through Greek) and the Arabic script, and possibly the Brahmic family of scripts (through Aramaic, Phoenician, and Greek).[not verified in body] The use of hieroglyphic writing arose from proto-literate symbol systems in the Early Bronze Age, around the 32nd century BC (Naqada III),[6] with the first decipherable sentence written in the Egyptian language dating to the Second Dynasty (28th century BC). Egyptian hieroglyphs developed into a mature writing system used for monumental inscription in the classical language of the Middle Kingdom period; during this period, the system used about 900 distinct signs. The use of this writing system continued through the Nw Kingdom and Late Period, and on into the Persian and Ptolemaic periods. Late survivals of hieroglyphic use are found well into the Roman period, extending into the 4th century AD.[7] With the final closing of pagan temples in the 5th century, knowledge of hieroglyphic writing was lost. Although attempts were made, the script remained undeciphered throughout the Middle Ages and the early modern period. The decipherment of hieroglyphic writing was finally accomplished in the 1820s by Jean-François Champollion, with the help of the Rosetta Stone.[8] The number of words contained in al Ancient Egyptian (i.e. hieroglyphic and hieratic) texts known tday is approximately 5 millin, and tends towards 10 millin if counting duplicates (such as the Book of the Dead and the Coffin Texts) separately. The most complete compendium of Ancient Egyptian, Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache, contains 1.5–1.7 millin words.[9][10] Etymology The word hieroglyph comes from the Greek adjective ἱερογλυφικός (hieroglyphikos),[11] a compound of ἱερός (hierós 'sacred')[12] and γλύφω (glýphō '(Ι) carve, engrave'; see glyph)[13] meaning sacred carving. The glyphs themselves, since the Ptolemaic period, were called τὰ ἱερογλυφικὰ [γράμματα] (tà hieroglyphikà [grámmata]) "the sacred engraved letters", the Greek counterpart to the Egyptian expression of mdw.w-nṯr "god's words".[14] Greek ἱερόγλυφος meant "a carver of hieroglyphs".[15] In English, hieroglyph as a noun is recorded from 1590, originally short for nominalized hieroglyphic (1580s, with a plural hieroglyphics), from adjectival use (hieroglyphic character).[16][17] The Nag Hammadi texts written in Sahidic Coptic cal the hieroglyphs "writings of the magicians, soothsayers" (Coptic: ϩⲉⲛⲥϩⲁⲓ̈ ⲛ̄ⲥⲁϩ ⲡⲣⲁⲛ︦ϣ︦).[18]

The later hieratic and demotic Egyptian scripts were derived from hieroglyphic writing, as was the Proto-Sinaitic script that later evolved into the Phoenician alphabet.[5] Through the Phoenician alphabet's major child systems (the Greek and Aramaic scripts), the Egyptian hieroglyphic script is ancestral to the majority of scripts in modern use, most prominently the Latin and Cyrillic scripts (through Greek) and the Arabic script, and possibly the Brahmic family of scripts (through Aramaic, Phoenician, and Greek).[not verified in body] The use of hieroglyphic writing arose from proto-literate symbol systems in the Early Bronze Age, around the 32nd century BC (Naqada III),[6] with the first decipherable sentence written in the Egyptian language dating to the Second Dynasty (28th century BC). Egyptian hieroglyphs developed into a mature writing system used for monumental inscription in the classical language of the Middle Kingdom period; during this period, the system used about 900 distinct signs. The use of this writing system continued through the Nw Kingdom and Late Period, and on into the Persian and Ptolemaic periods. Late survivals of hieroglyphic use are found well into the Roman period, extending into the 4th century AD.[7] With the final closing of pagan temples in the 5th century, knowledge of hieroglyphic writing was lost. Although attempts were made, the script remained undeciphered throughout the Middle Ages and the early modern period.
